name: Data Structures
description: Arrays, hash tables, trees, heaps, graphs and tries — how they are built, what they cost, and when to pick which.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Data Structures is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is a data structure?
cards.answer: A way of organising data in memory so that the operations you need — lookup, insertion, ordering, finding neighbours — are efficient. Choosing the right one often matters more than clever code.
cards.explanation: Every data structure is a trade-off: a hash map makes lookups by key fast but forgets order; a sorted array makes searching fast but inserting slow. Knowing the trade-offs is the core skill.

cards.prompt: What is an array (or list)?
cards.answer: An ordered collection of elements stored one after another and accessed by index — `items[0]` is the first. Reading any index is instant, O(1); inserting in the middle is slow, O(n), because later elements must shift.
cards.explanation: Most languages' everyday list type (Python `list`, JavaScript `Array`, Java `ArrayList`, Go slice) is a dynamic array that grows by reallocating a bigger block. Indexes usually start at 0.

cards.prompt: What is a hash map (dictionary)?
cards.answer: A collection of key → value pairs with very fast lookup by key — O(1) on average. A hash function turns each key into a position in an internal array.
cards.explanation: Called `dict` in Python, `Map`/object in JavaScript, `HashMap` in Java and `map` in Go. Use one whenever you find yourself searching a list for a matching item: counting words, caching results, indexing records by id.

cards.prompt: Stack vs queue
cards.answer: A stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO); a queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO).

left.title: Stack (LIFO)
points: push adds to the top, pop removes from the top

right.title: Queue (FIFO)
points: enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front
Like a line at a shop

cards.explanation: Both restrict how you access data, and that restriction is the point: it makes the order of processing explicit and every operation O(1).

cards.prompt: What is a tree, in data structures?
cards.answer: A hierarchy of nodes: one root at the top, each node having child nodes, and nodes with no children called leaves. There are no cycles, so every node has exactly one parent (except the root).
cards.explanation: Trees are everywhere: file systems, the HTML DOM, organisation charts, JSON documents. A binary search tree keeps values ordered so search takes O(log n) when it is balanced.

cards.prompt: What is a graph, in data structures?
cards.answer: A set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. Edges can be directed (one-way, like following someone) or undirected (two-way, like friendship), and can carry weights (like road distances).
cards.explanation: Graphs model networks of any kind: social networks, road maps, web links, package dependencies. A tree is a special graph with no cycles.

modules.name: Linear Structures
modules.description: Arrays, lists, stacks, queues and the cache behaviour that decides real performance.

cards.prompt: Dynamic array vs linked list
cards.answer: Arrays give O(1) indexing and cache locality; linked lists give O(1) splice at a known node and stable references.

right.title: Linked list
points: Pointer chasing — a cache miss per node

cards.explanation: In practice arrays win far more often than the asymptotics suggest, because a cache miss costs ~100x an L1 hit. Linked lists earn their place when you hold stable node references, splice frequently, or need intrusive lists in kernels and allocators.

cards.prompt: Why is appending to a dynamic array amortised O(1) even though resizing is O(n)?
cards.answer: Because capacity grows geometrically. Doubling means the total copy work across n appends is n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n, so the average per append is constant.
cards.explanation: Growing by a constant amount instead would make n appends O(n²). The growth factor trades memory for copies: 2x wastes up to half the buffer, 1.5x reuses freed blocks better — which is why several implementations chose it.

cards.prompt: You are parsing nested brackets and separately scheduling jobs fairly. Which structure for each, and why?
cards.answer: A stack (LIFO) for the brackets — the most recent opener must close first. A queue (FIFO) for the jobs — fairness means first submitted, first served.
cards.explanation: Recursion is a stack; breadth-first traversal is a queue; depth-first is a stack. Recognising which discipline a problem needs usually solves half of it. A deque supports both ends and is the base for sliding-window algorithms.

cards.prompt: How do hash tables resolve collisions, and what is the load factor?
cards.answer: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a per-bucket list or tree; open addressing probes for another slot (linear, quadratic or double hashing). Load factor = entries / buckets, and it drives the resize.
cards.explanation: Open addressing is cache-friendlier but degrades sharply past ~0.7 load and needs tombstones on delete. Chaining tolerates higher load and simpler deletion. Java upgrades long chains to red-black trees to bound the worst case at O(log n).

cards.prompt: Hash table insert, lookup and delete complexity?
cards.answer: O(1) average, O(n) worst case; O(n) space.
cards.explanation: The worst case needs every key in one bucket — possible with adversarial input, which is why languages randomise string hashing per process (hash-flooding DoS). Ordering is not guaranteed; use a tree map or an insertion-ordered map when it matters.

modules.name: Trees, Heaps & Tries
modules.description: Balanced search trees, priority queues, prefix trees and the structures databases are built on.

cards.prompt: Why does an unbalanced BST matter, and how do balanced trees fix it?
cards.answer: Inserting sorted data into a plain BST produces a linked list — O(n) operations. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) rotate on insert/delete to keep height O(log n).
cards.explanation: AVL is more strictly balanced (faster lookups, more rotations); red-black tolerates more imbalance (faster writes) and is what most standard libraries use for ordered maps. B-trees generalise the idea to high fan-out for disk and page-based storage.

cards.prompt: Why do databases index with B+ trees rather than red-black trees?
cards.answer: Because the cost unit is a disk or page read, not a comparison. A B+ tree node holds hundreds of keys in one page, so tree height is tiny — three or four page reads for millions of rows — and leaves are linked for range scans.
cards.explanation: A red-black tree with a million rows is ~20 levels, meaning up to 20 random reads. A B+ tree with fan-out 500 is 3 levels. Storing all values in the leaves and chaining them also makes `BETWEEN` and `ORDER BY` scans sequential.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — Anatomy of an index

cards.prompt: Binary heap: push, pop-min and peek complexity? And building a heap from n items?
cards.answer: Push O(log n), pop O(log n), peek O(1). Heapify from an array is O(n), not O(n log n).

complexity.time: push/pop O(log n), peek O(1), build O(n)

cards.explanation: A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array: children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, so no pointers. The O(n) build works bottom-up — most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a level or two. It backs Dijkstra, A*, schedulers and top-k.

cards.prompt: You need autocomplete over millions of terms with prefix matching. Which structure, and what is the trade-off?
cards.answer: A trie (prefix tree): lookup and prefix enumeration cost O(k) in the key length, independent of the number of stored keys. The cost is memory — one node per character unless compressed.
cards.explanation: A radix/PATRICIA trie collapses single-child chains and cuts memory dramatically. For static dictionaries, a DAWG or an FST (as used by Lucene) compresses shared suffixes too. A hash map cannot answer prefix queries at all.

cards.prompt: Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix
cards.answer: List is O(V+E) space and fast to iterate neighbours; matrix is O(V²) space and O(1) edge lookup.

left.title: Adjacency list
points: Right for sparse graphs — most real graphs

right.title: Adjacency matrix
points: Right for dense graphs and small V

cards.explanation: Real-world graphs (social, road, dependency) are sparse: E ≈ cV, so lists win by orders of magnitude. Matrices shine when V is small and bounded, or when you want bitset tricks or Floyd–Warshall.

cards.prompt: What does a disjoint-set (union-find) structure do, and what makes it near-constant time?
cards.answer: It tracks a partition of elements into disjoint sets with `find` (which set?) and `union` (merge two). Path compression plus union by rank/size gives O(α(n)) amortised — inverse Ackermann, effectively constant.
cards.explanation: It powers Kruskal's MST, connected-component labelling, cycle detection in undirected graphs, and incremental connectivity. Path compression flattens the tree during every find, so repeated queries get cheaper as you use it.

cards.prompt: You want to avoid a disk lookup for keys that are definitely absent, using very little memory. What do you use?
cards.answer: A Bloom filter: k hash functions over a bit array. It answers 'definitely not present' or 'possibly present' — false positives are possible, false negatives are not.
cards.explanation: About 10 bits per element gives ~1% false positives. Standard Bloom filters cannot delete (counting variants can) and cannot be resized. LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra and Chrome's safe-browsing all use them to skip expensive lookups.

cards.prompt: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. Which two structures do you combine?
cards.answer: A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordering nodes by recency. Get moves the node to the head; put evicts the tail when full.
cards.explanation: The hash map gives O(1) lookup, the linked list gives O(1) reordering and eviction — neither can do both alone. This is the canonical 'compose two structures' interview question, and it is exactly how real caches are built.

modules.name: Sets, Queues & Traversals
modules.description: Set algebra, priority queues, ring buffers, tree traversals and choosing the right structure.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: Sets give O(1) average membership plus set algebra: intersection `&`, union `|`, difference `-` and symmetric difference `^`. They deduplicate for free and turn "is x in this list?" from O(n) into O(1). Elements must be hashable, and iteration order is not guaranteed — hence the `sorted` calls.

cards.prompt: A job scheduler must always run the highest-priority pending job next, while jobs keep arriving. Which structure?
cards.answer: A priority queue, implemented as a binary heap: O(log n) insert, O(log n) remove-highest, O(1) peek. A sorted list would make every insert O(n).
cards.explanation: Break ties with an insertion counter so equal-priority jobs stay FIFO and items never need to be compared directly — Python's `heapq` idiom is pushing `(priority, counter, job)`. Changing a priority in place needs an indexed heap or lazy deletion (push a new entry, skip stale ones on pop).

cards.prompt: What is a ring (circular) buffer, and where is it used?
cards.answer: A fixed-size array with head and tail indices that wrap around modulo the capacity, giving O(1) enqueue and dequeue with no allocation. When full, it either rejects writes or overwrites the oldest entry.
cards.explanation: Ring buffers are everywhere bounded memory matters: audio and network I/O buffers, kernel log buffers, "last N events" telemetry, and lock-free single-producer single-consumer queues. Power-of-two capacities let `index & (n - 1)` replace the modulo.

cards.prompt: For this BST, what do in-order, pre-order and post-order traversals print?
cards.explanation: In-order (left, node, right) visits a BST in sorted order. Pre-order (node first) is how you serialise or copy a tree; post-order (node last) is how you delete one or evaluate an expression tree. Level-order is BFS with a queue.

cards.prompt: Balanced BST (red-black, AVL): cost of search, insert, delete, min/max, and in-order iteration of all n keys?
cards.answer: Search, insert and delete O(log n); min/max O(log n) (O(1) if cached); full ordered iteration O(n).

complexity.time: O(log n) search/insert/delete; O(n) full iteration

cards.explanation: Balanced trees trade the hash table's O(1) average for guaranteed O(log n) and ordering — which buys floor/ceiling queries, range scans and sorted iteration. That is why `TreeMap`, `std::map` and database indexes use trees rather than hashes.

cards.prompt: Pick a structure for each: (a) dedupe a million user IDs, (b) "undo" in an editor, (c) keep the 10 most recent log lines, (d) find all words with a prefix, (e) answer "which users are within this price range" repeatedly.
cards.answer: (a) hash set, (b) stack, (c) ring buffer / bounded deque, (d) trie, (e) balanced tree or sorted array with binary search (a B-tree index in a database).
cards.explanation: Name the operations first — lookup, ordered iteration, range queries, push/pop at which end — then pick the structure whose cheap operations match. Most performance problems in application code are a list used where a set or map belonged.

modules.name: Advanced & Probabilistic Structures
modules.description: Fenwick and segment trees, skip lists, HyperLogLog, count-min sketch and persistent structures.

cards.prompt: Fenwick (binary indexed) tree vs segment tree
cards.answer: Both answer range queries while supporting updates in O(log n), where a plain prefix-sum array needs O(n) per update.

left.title: Fenwick tree
points: Array of n cells, index tricks with `i & -i`
Point update + prefix query O(log n)

right.title: Segment tree
points: Any associative op: min, max, gcd

cards.explanation: A Fenwick tree is tiny and fast for invertible aggregates like sums; a segment tree handles anything associative (min, max, gcd) and, with lazy propagation, range updates. They power leaderboards, order statistics and competitive-programming range problems.

cards.prompt: What is a skip list, and why do Redis sorted sets use one?
cards.answer: A sorted linked list with extra "express lane" levels: each node is promoted to the next level with probability ½, so search skips most nodes — O(log n) expected for search, insert and delete, with no rebalancing rotations.
cards.explanation: Skip lists are simpler than balanced trees, support range scans naturally, and are easier to make concurrent (lock-free variants exist, such as Java's `ConcurrentSkipListMap`). Redis combines a skip list with a hash table for sorted sets.

cards.prompt: You need the number of distinct visitors per page across billions of events, with a tiny memory budget. What do you use?
cards.answer: HyperLogLog: it hashes each item and tracks the maximum run of leading zeros in buckets, estimating cardinality with ~1–2% error in about 12 KB — regardless of how many distinct items there are.
cards.explanation: HLL sketches merge by taking the maximum per bucket, so per-day or per-shard counts combine exactly into totals. Redis (`PFADD`/`PFCOUNT`), BigQuery `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` and most analytics systems use it. Exact distinct counts would need memory proportional to the distinct set.

cards.prompt: What does a count-min sketch estimate, and in which direction is it wrong?
cards.answer: The frequency of items in a stream, using a small 2-D array of counters and several hash functions: increment one counter per row, and estimate by taking the minimum across rows. It can overestimate (collisions add counts) but never underestimates.
cards.explanation: It answers "roughly how often has X occurred?" and heavy-hitter questions — top URLs, abusive IPs — in fixed memory. Like Bloom filters, its error is one-sided and tunable by width and depth.

cards.prompt: How can an immutable (persistent) data structure be efficient if every update returns a new version?
cards.answer: Structural sharing: an update copies only the path from the root to the changed node (O(log n) nodes in a tree), and the new version shares every other node with the old one. Both versions stay valid and cheap.
cards.explanation: This is how Clojure vectors, Scala and Immutable.js collections, and git trees work. You get free snapshots, undo history and thread safety without locks. The cost is some constant-factor overhead compared to a mutable array.
